title: The state machine
sub: What the compiler turns await into
cards/0/title: await isn't magic, it's a switch
cards/0/body:
The compiler rewrites an async method into a struct: a state machine. Local variables become its fields, and the method body becomes a MoveNext function with the step number kept in a state field.

Every await is a spot where MoveNext can return and later come back.
cards/1/task: The responses are still on their way. Step through MoveNext and count the calls and pauses.
cards/2/q: How many times is MoveNext called for a method with two awaits if neither task is ready?
cards/2/explain: The first call is the start, then one more for each continuation after an await.
cards/3/q: Why isn't variable a lost between MoveNext calls?
cards/3/options/0: It became a field of the state machine
cards/3/explain: The stack frame disappears between calls, but the struct's fields stay.
cards/4/task: Turn on "Results are ready" and walk through again.
cards/5/q: The results were already ready. How many pauses were there?
cards/5/explain: IsCompleted = true, so the method runs straight through in a single MoveNext call.
cards/6/title: On the stack, then on the heap
cards/6/body: In Release the state machine is a struct and lives on the stack as long as the method never pauses. On the first real pause it moves to the heap so it can outlive the method's return.
cards/6/deep: In .NET Core 2.1+ the state machine's "box" is the task itself: AsyncStateMachineBox derives from Task<T>, so a pause costs a single allocation. In Debug the state machine is a class so that Edit and Continue works.
cards/7/q: What does MoveNext do when it meets an incomplete awaiter?
cards/7/items/1: Writes the step number to state
cards/7/items/2: Subscribes MoveNext to completion via AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted
cards/7/explain: That's how a method "pauses" without holding a thread.
cards/8/pairs/1/1: Runs a piece of the method up to the next await
cards/8/pairs/2/1: What we're waiting on right now
